facts.value: Four-page covering report to Audit Committee, 20 July 2026 (report ref AC260720). Author Charlotte Spendley, Director of Resources. Summarises treasury activity for the year ending 31 March 2026 (2025/26 outturn). Recommendation is to note. Appendices A (Investments Portfolio), B (CFR & Borrowing Portfolio), C (Prudential Indicators) and D (PIS properties) are LISTED but NOT INCLUDED in the local PDF — the tabular detail (loan-by-loan schedule, full CFR breakdown, full prudential indicators) sits there and is not held for this note.
facts.note: Covering report carries several headline figures in the body text — loan-book total, the two new PWLB draws (principals only, not rates), investment balances, one CFR-related number, the NFC/NRS ratio, Property Fund value — but the tabular detail is in the appendices we don't hold. This is a paper that CAN be written on because the loan-book reconciliation ties from the numbers in the body text alone.

facts.value: £53.5m at 31 March 2026 (up £24.7m from £28.8m at 31 March 2025). Increase 'largely represented by two new Public Works Loan Board loans of £12.5 and £15.0m respectively'.
facts.note: The two new PWLB loans identified in the paper reconcile to our file exactly. Our file has them as 911340 MATURITY £12,500,000 at 4.51% maturing 10 March 2027, and 915847 MATURITY £15,000,000 at 4.69% maturing 25 March 2027. Together £27.5m — £2.8m higher than the £24.7m net year-on-year increase, consistent with annuity paydown on the other seven long loans in the book.

facts.value: TIES. Our file: 9 PWLB loans totalling £53,485,293 at weighted 3.3545% as at 31 March 2026. Paper para 10: £53.5m. Difference £15k — a rounding tie. Two named new PWLB loans (£12.5m and £15.0m in the paper) match to the pound in our file (911340 £12,500,000; 915847 £15,000,000).
facts.note: Safe to open the email with this reconciliation. Our file also confirms the two-loan detail behind the paper's £12.5m and £15.0m — including the maturity dates (both March 2027) and coupons (4.51%, 4.69%) which the paper does not print.

facts.value: Bifurcated shape: 51.4% of the £53.5m book (£27.5m) matures inside 12 months — both loans in a 15-day window in March 2027. Other 48.6% (£25,985,293) runs 30–50 years and averages just over 2%. Nothing in between.
facts.note: Bucket detail from our file: under 12 months 2 loans £27,500,000 at 4.608% weighted; 25 years and over 7 loans £25,985,293 at 2.028% weighted. Nothing in the 1-25 year buckets. This is a striking barbell shape driven by the recent bridging of a £23.5m RDCHC advance (see rdchc_exposure) with short PWLB. The March 2027 refi date is 7 months from today (16 August 2026) — the hardest, most dated single event in the paper.

facts.value: £22.06m at 31 March 2026: £17.06m short-term call accounts + £5.00m Property Funds (of which CCLA and, until closure in year, Hermes). Property Fund value stated separately at para 15 as £4.636m.
facts.note: Para 3 gives Q3 2025/26 comparators for the call accounts as £19.9m and £14.9m — the two numbers within the same phrase are not fully aligned in the paper text; reproduced verbatim in the extract. Property Fund is at para 15 (£4.636m 'currently') — small delta from the £5.00m rounded figure at para 3 as at 31 March 2026, consistent with fair-value drift over 3–4 months. Statutory override on IFRS 9 pooled fund treatment applied (CCLA named at para 16).

facts.value: £33.03m loan to Rother DC Housing Company (RDCHC) at 31 March 2026, plus £2.595m interest accrued to date. Loan grew £23.5m in year on a Development Facility Agreement entered March 2025 (replaced prior Working Capital Agreement). Rate on the loan is NOT disclosed in the covering report.

source.title: Treasury Management Update — Outturn 2025/26, para 4; risk framing at para 22

facts.note: Total RDCHC exposure = £35.6m (principal £33.03m + accrued £2.595m). Interest yielded from RDCHC in year was £1.87m (para 5, kept separate from the £646,681 headline investment interest). Para 22 flags this as a member-known risk 'especially as we reach the peak debt position and the interest has been accrued for'. Third-party single-name concentration on the balance sheet. The lending arrangement to RDCHC (rate, maturity, security) sits outside the paper and outside the platform — this is 'company_lending' territory in the schema vocabulary.

facts.value: £646,681 in 2025/26 (excluding £1.87m interest accrued from RDCHC) vs a full-year budget of £1.214m. Q3 print (excluding RDCHC): £528,000. Split (pie chart, para 8): Housing company 74%, Lloyds accounts 17%, CCLA 8%, Hermes 1%.
facts.note: £567k under budget. Two named drivers: Hermes Property Fund performance and subsequent closure; lower cash balances due to capital programme and RDCHC investment. If RDCHC interest were added to yielded interest the total would be £2.52m — above budget — but the paper keeps them separated (RDCHC accrual, not cash yielded).

facts.value: The paper's only CFR-related number is at para 9: 'The outturn position for the year was £44.6m compared to the £42.9m projected at the beginning of 2025/26 for in-year spend.' Given external borrowing at £53.5m exceeds £44.6m, this reads more naturally as capital programme spend outturn (of which 37% = ~£16.5m is borrowing-supported per the same paragraph) rather than the year-end CFR balance. Actual CFR balance sits in Appendix B, not held.
facts.note: The phrasing is ambiguous enough that I would not cite a Rother CFR figure in outreach without seeing Appendix B. Do not raise this in the email — it invites correction on something we haven't fully read. Internal note only.

facts.value: Original 2025/26 budget forecast 1.1%; outturn 8.13% (para 14). Paper attributes the overshoot to 'the improved interest receivable position noted above'.
facts.note: INTERNAL ONLY. The paper's explanation reads oddly — a higher receivable position would normally REDUCE net financing costs (numerator), thus LOWER the ratio, not raise it 7 points. Possible readings: (a) receivable being counted as negative revenue (raising numerator or shrinking denominator), (b) the RDCHC interest accrued netted somewhere that distorts the ratio, (c) Rother uses a non-standard definition. Full indicator table would be in Appendix C, not held. Do not raise in the email — would be inviting a correction on a definitional point that we cannot resolve from the covering report alone.

facts.value: Approved 7 April 2025 as part of TMSS; revised at Full Council 18 May 2026 as part of 2026/27 TMSS — 'authorised limit and operational boundary were reduced to reflect our current programme and priorities' (para 13). Actual borrowing 'comfortably within both limits (and would have been comfortably within the revised limits)'. Numerical limits sit in Appendix C, not held.
facts.note: Direction of travel is worth noting: the Council REDUCED its authorised limit and operational boundary at the May 2026 TMSS refresh 'to reflect our current programme and priorities'. That is compatible with the paragraph 11 stance ('use internal balances where possible to minimise borrowing costs') but not with the appearance that they've overshot underlying need in 2025/26. Without Appendix C we can't tell the new limits.

facts.value: NOT CLEANLY CHECKABLE from this paper. External borrowing = £53.5m (para 10). CFR figure at para 9 (£44.6m) is ambiguous — likely capital programme spend, not year-end CFR balance. Other long-term liabilities not disclosed in covering report. Arithmetic on the £44.6m as CFR would give: 44.6 − 53.5 − (OLTL assumed 0) = -£8.9m (over-borrowed by £8.9m), which conflicts with the paragraph 11 stance. More likely reading: CFR balance lives in Appendix B and is materially higher, and the identity holds — but we can't demonstrate that from this paper.
facts.note: Not cited in the email. Recorded here to demonstrate the identity was tested and not resolvable from the covering report.
Named at para 6: 'Advice will be sought from MUFG Treasury Services as appropriate.' Do not name the advisor in the email — noted here for context only.

summary.text:
Four-page covering report to Audit Committee on 20 July 2026 (report ref AC260720), authored by Charlotte Spendley, Director of Resources. Summarises 2025/26 treasury activity. The appendices — A (Investments Portfolio), B (CFR & Borrowing Portfolio), C (Prudential Indicators) and D (PIS properties) — are listed on the cover but not included in the local PDF, so the loan-by-loan schedule, the CFR balance and the full prudential indicator set are not held for this note. The covering report itself carries enough headline figures to work on: the loan-book total (para 10), the two new PWLB draws (£12.5m and £15.0m — principals only, not rates), the investment split (£17.06m calls plus £5m Property Funds, para 3), the RDCHC exposure (£33.03m + £2.595m accrued interest, para 4), and the NFC/NRS ratio (8.13% outturn against 1.1% budget, para 14).

The loan-book reconciliation is the clean thing. Our file carries 9 PWLB loans for Rother totalling £53,485,293 at a weighted 3.3545% as at 31 March 2026 — ties to para 10's £53.5m to within £15k, a rounding tie. Better still, the two named new PWLB loans in the paper (£12.5m and £15.0m) sit in our file to the pound: 911340 MATURITY £12,500,000 at 4.51% maturing 10 March 2027, and 915847 MATURITY £15,000,000 at 4.69% maturing 25 March 2027. Coupons and dates come from our file, not the paper. The shape of the book is striking: 51.4% (£27.5m) matures inside 12 months, and both loans fall in a 15-day window in March 2027; the other 48.6% (seven long-dated loans, £25,985,293) runs to 2069–2071, averaging 2.028% weighted — profile mix within that bucket is 6 ANNUITY plus 1 MATURITY. Nothing in the 1–25-year buckets. A pure barbell.

The balance-sheet identity is not cleanly checkable from this paper. The only CFR-related figure is at para 9 (£44.6m 'outturn position for the year… for in-year spend') and reads more naturally as capital programme spend outturn than the year-end CFR balance — external borrowing of £53.5m already exceeds it, and taking £44.6m as CFR with zero OLTL would give an over-borrowed position of £8.9m that would sit oddly against para 11's 'use internal balances where possible' stance. Appendix B is where this resolves; not held. Not raised in the email.

Email drafted and ready to send to Charlotte Spendley at Charlotte.spendley@rother.gov.uk (published on page 4 of the paper). The hook is the March 2027 refinancing lump — a hard, dated event on 51% of the debt just over seven months from the meeting date, on a book we can describe loan-by-loan. The break-cost position on the long legacy book (net discount ~£11m indicative) is described in relative terms only, without the headline total, and with the standard disclaimers on indicative pricing and the DMO's sole authority to quote. NFC/NRS oddity (8.13% vs 1.1% budgeted) and the CFR ambiguity are held back as internal-only observations — both invite correction on things we haven't fully read.

officer.body:
Hi Charlotte,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your Treasury Management Update – Outturn 2025/26 that went to Audit Committee on 20 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 9 PWLB loans for Rother totalling £53,485,293 at a weighted 3.35%, which matches your paragraph 10 print of £53.5m to within £15,000. Better than that, the two new PWLB loans your paragraph names — £12.5m and £15.0m — sit in our file to the pound: £12,500,000 at 4.51% maturing 10 March 2027, and £15,000,000 at 4.69% maturing 25 March 2027. So the book we describe below is the same one you're looking at.

The thing that most stands out in that book is the shape. £27.5m of the £53.5m sits inside twelve months — both loans mature in a fifteen-day window in March 2027. The other £26.0m runs to 2069–2071 and averages just over 2%. There isn't anything in between. That leaves one hard, dated refinancing event just over seven months out, on 51% of the book. On today's DMO premature-repayment curve the two March 2027 loans sit at slight premiums, which is a compact way of saying the short-end rate today is fractionally below the 4.5–4.7% coupons you're paying — so a same-tenor roll today would clear in roughly the same rate band, subject to what the curve does between now and March. We publish the whole PWLB curve at both fixings, and the monthly breakdown of every loan the sector actually draws, at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

The other side of that page is the legacy book. Your seven long-dated loans running out to 2069–2071 average 2.03% across £26m of principal. On the DMO's premature-repayment curve those loans carry very large discounts today — the four largest are indicatively £4.2m, £3.0m, £2.7m and £0.6m below principal. Whether that means anything depends on what would replace them; replacement cost, MRP treatment and the wider capital plan all sit outside our model, and only the DMO can give a binding early-repayment quote. Your own book priced daily against that curve is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Everything on it is indicative — not a quote.

One standing thing worth mentioning: our liability benchmark pathway is interactive and built on live data, which matters given CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates. Your Appendix B is where the CFR and borrowing portfolio sit — the two inputs the benchmark needs. The interactive version is at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark and rebuilds live off the curve.

On training, three fit. Strategic PWLB borrowing sits directly behind the March 2027 refi question. The Liability Benchmark: using it in practice course goes to the ratio between underlying capital need and the external position — the same thing your paragraph 11 stance ("use internal balances where possible to minimise borrowing costs") is describing. And Reading the quarterly & outturn reports is a members' course written for the committee this paper goes to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
